parts.title: Wild red foxes eating other animals' droppings: DNA tests in droppings reveal a way of life that may be common among animals
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Animals with backbones are known to eat the droppings of other species. Yet we still do not know what this habit does for the way species live alongside each other, partly because it is so hard to prove. We collected droppings from red foxes and pine martens over a large area and used a DNA test that reads the DNA of every animal in a sample at once. We found dog DNA in a large share of the red fox droppings, and we asked whether foxes were getting it by eating dog droppings.

We checked several other explanations. The dog DNA might have come from mistakes in our lab work, or from some other source. We also compared how often dog DNA turned up with how often the fox's main prey, the short-tailed field vole, turned up. Finally, we considered whether foxes could be getting dog DNA by killing or eating dogs. We also measured how much energy dog droppings contain by burning them in a sealed container and measuring the heat.

Three things point to dog droppings as the source of the dog DNA in fox droppings: dog DNA was common in fox droppings, it became more common at the same time as voles became less common, and the two tended to move in opposite directions. Dog droppings hold a lot of energy, and we found that foxes, but not pine martens, regularly eat them. Foxes seem to use them as a backup food when their usual prey is scarce.

A few scattered reports in earlier studies may suggest that eating other species' droppings is a common and widespread way that animals with backbones interact. However, more work should find out how common this is in other places and what it means for the wider community of living things. Tools such as DNA testing in droppings offer a way forward.
parts.introduction_first: A central goal of ecology, the science of how living things relate to each other and their surroundings, is to understand how the ways species interact shape which species live together in a community and how that community changes over time (Begon et al., 2005). Predators, parasites, parasitoids (insects whose young grow inside a host and eventually kill it) and plant-eaters all harm the animals or plants they feed on, though by different amounts. The effects of these harmful interactions are generally well understood (Krebs, 2008). Some interactions between species do not harm the individuals involved. These can help one or both species, either by helping both sides (mutualism) or by helping one side without affecting the other (commensalism) (Mikula et al., 2018). Interest in these helpful interactions is growing, and people recognise that they may have far-reaching effects on whole communities of living things. Even so, they have received far less attention than harmful ones, and most of the research has focused on plants (Bronstein, 2009; Bruno et al., 2003).
parts.introduction_rest:
Among animals with backbones, one example of a helpful interaction is when larger predators leave the remains of their prey, partly eaten, for scavengers to feed on. This affects how species interact and how they manage to live alongside each other (Moleón et al., 2014; Wilson & Wolkovich, 2011). Still, it is not simple to say whether leaving these carcasses is mostly helpful or mostly harmful for the animals that use them. It has two sides: it gives them food, but it also brings a risk of being killed (Prugh & Sivy, 2020).

Eating another species' droppings could be a helpful interaction. That would be the case if the droppings are a valuable source of energy and nutrients, if the animal actually uses them as food, and if the benefits of doing so outweigh the risks. Yet the role of droppings as a way for animals with backbones to interact has received little attention (but see Rowland, 1975).

Animals are well known to eat their own droppings. One example is caecotrophy, in which an animal eats its own droppings after they have been fermented in the caecum, a pouch in the gut (see Hirakawa, 2001). In contrast, reports of animals eating other species' droppings are still scarce and often come from chance sightings rather than careful study. This is partly because it is hard to prove in practice (e.g., Gallant, 2004; Nishikawa & Mochida, 2010; Yong, 2018).

Like caecotrophy, eating other species' droppings may meet animals' essential needs. For example, Egyptian vultures (Neophron percnopterus Savigny) are reported to get the carotenes, orange-yellow pigments, that they need for their facial markings from dung pads left by hoofed animals (Negro et al., 2002). In the same way, scientists have suggested that small perching birds may get calcium from bones found in the droppings of meat-eating animals (Gallant, 2004; Payne, 1972).

Other species may eat droppings only when they happen to come along, rather than as a regular habit. Seabirds such as pale-faced sheathbills (Chionis albus Gmelin), Wilson's storm petrels (Oceanites oceanicus Kuhl), kelp gulls (Larus dominicanus Lichtenstein) and dolphin gulls (Leucophaeus scoresbii Traill) have all been seen feeding on seal and whale droppings (Favero, 1996; Kraus & Stone, 1995; Seguel et al., 2017). Domestic dogs (Canis lupus familiaris) living freely in India, Ethiopia and Zimbabwe have also been recorded eating human droppings (Atickem et al., 2010; Butler et al., 2018; Vanak & Gompper, 2009). Importantly, human droppings held as much energy and nutrition as other foods the dogs could reach, or more (Butler et al., 2018).

Droppings from other species may also be a backup food when other foods are fairly scarce. In Svalbard, a group of Arctic islands, reindeer (Rangifer tarandus platyrhynchus Vrolik) readily eat barnacle goose droppings during the short summer. Grotto salamanders (Eurycea spelaea Stejneger) live in caves that are naturally poor in nutrients, and they switched to eating gray bat (Myotis grisescens Howell) droppings during the bats' breeding season. Plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae Hodgson) eat large amounts of domestic yak (Bos grunniens Linnaeus) droppings to survive the winter (Fenolio et al., 2005; Speakman et al., 2021; van der Wal & Loonen, 1998). In all these very different cases, the animals eat droppings when food is scarce, either in a particular place (Svalbard, the caves) or at a particular time of year (winter), and the droppings offer a valuable food that is easy to digest. Beyond these scattered examples, we do not know whether eating other species' droppings is a widespread and ecologically important interaction in animal communities across the world's major natural regions, such as forests, grasslands and deserts, even though it may be overlooked.

It is rarely possible to measure how common this habit is by watching animals directly or by examining what is in their guts and the hard remains in their droppings. The exceptions are when animals live in stable colonies, when droppings can still be recognised (for example, when they have only just been passed), or when the droppings contain hard remains that must have come from eating droppings (Butler et al., 2018; e.g., toilet paper, Nishikawa & Mochida, 2010; Seguel et al., 2017; Speakman et al., 2021). Newer methods that look for DNA in droppings, such as the DNA test that reads the DNA of every animal in a sample at once, could reveal that animals have eaten droppings even when no remains can be seen (Speakman et al., 2021; Taberlet, Coissac, et al., 2012). However, this has hardly been tested.

In this study, we used a large DNA test of the diet of meat-eating mammals in Scotland to explore whether dog droppings are a backup food for red foxes (Vulpes vulpes L.) when wild prey are scarce. We tested several possible explanations for why dog DNA turns up in fox droppings: (i) foxes eating dog droppings, (ii) dogs rolling over fox droppings or urinating on them, or (iii) mistakes in the DNA test itself. We also discuss why killing or eating dogs is an unlikely explanation, given what earlier studies show and how often we found dog DNA.

We also measured how much energy dog droppings contain by burning them in a sealed container and measuring the heat. To test explanations (i) and (ii), we compared how often dog DNA and short-tailed field vole (Microtus agrestis Linnaeus) DNA turned up in fox droppings over four sampling seasons and 2 years. We then used a statistical method called regression to see whether the amount of dog DNA rose or fell along with the amount of field vole DNA. If dog DNA stayed at a steady level, or changed with the seasons, in the fox's diet and was not linked to how often field voles appeared, that would support dogs tampering with fox droppings as the source of the dog DNA. Instead, if dog DNA in the fox's diet went up or down as field voles went down or up, that would support foxes eating the droppings.

For explanation (iii), we counted how many places the dog and fox DNA sequences differed, and we looked at the pattern of dog and field vole DNA reads compared with fox DNA. A read is one short piece of DNA sequence recorded by the test. If foxes were getting dog DNA by eating dog droppings, the strength of the dog signal (the number of reads) should not be linked to the strength of the fox signal, and the two DNA sequences should differ a lot.
parts.methods:
## 2 Methods

### 2.1 Where we did the study

We carried out this study in the northwest of the Cairngorms National Park in Scotland (57°09′34″N, 03°51′40″W). The area has a temperate oceanic climate, which means mild temperatures and rain spread fairly evenly through the year. Much of the land is covered by seminatural forest of the kind known as Caledonian forest, which has grown there for a very long time. There are also plantations of Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) and areas where trees have been cut down completely, known as clear-felled areas (for details see Zalewska et al., 2021).

Field voles are the main prey of many meat-eating mammals in this area, including red foxes, which is the animal we studied here. Their numbers rise and fall in regular cycles (Lambin et al., 2000). Surveys of small mammals showed that there were few field voles around for the whole time we studied the foxes' diet, in 2018 and 2019.

### 2.2 Collecting the droppings

To find out what meat-eating mammals were eating, we collected droppings along transects, which are set lines that we walked along, on unpaved forest roads and trails. We did this at three to six sites (see below). Each site covered 6–11 km². We chose sites that gave us as many transects as possible and that varied in their habitats. We judged this variety by how much of the land was clear-felled or covered in grasses and other low plants, compared with forest, and by how much deer were being shot, because dead deer add dead animals to the area. The centres of neighbouring sites were at least 5 and at most 8 km apart.

We sampled from February to April and from May to July in 2018, and in the same months in 2019. These are the times of year that matter most to the animals: the first is a time of food shortage, and the second is the breeding season of the prey we were interested in. We call these two periods winter and spring.

In the first season we visited three sites, and in the second season we visited six. In the next two seasons we visited five. The first season had two visits, and we collected droppings on both. Each of the later seasons had three visits. On the first visit we cleared away the droppings, and on the next two we collected them, so that we could gather as many fresh samples as possible. On average, visits were 21 days apart, with a range from 12 to 48 days.

One or two surveyors walked side by side along the tracks and trails, looking for droppings. In the field, we identified each dropping as probably coming from a certain species by its size and shape (Summers et al., 2015). We used disposable wooden sticks to take about 1 cm³ of droppings from each of 2887 samples. We put this into 95% ethanol (a strong alcohol) and then moved it into silica gel, a material that soaks up moisture, or we put it straight into silica gel.

Volunteers also collected 298 samples. These were frozen whole, and 1 cm³ was moved into silica gel up to 18 months later. Another 232 samples came from an existing study that was still going on at one of our sites. These were also frozen whole and were collected on a single visit, which happened to be the last visit of our sampling seasons.

In total we had 3417 samples. We chose 2084 of them for DNA testing in droppings, picking them so that we covered as many places and times as possible, and so that each sample was a separate meal. We included every sample that we had probably identified in the field as fox (763) or Eurasian badger (Meles meles L.; 85). We also included some of the samples we had tentatively identified in the field as pine marten (Martes martes L.; 973), least weasel or stoat (Mustela erminea and Mustela nivalis L.; 213), and samples we could not identify (50). Text S1 in Appendix S1 gives more details on how we chose the samples.

### 2.3 DNA testing in droppings

We used DNA testing in droppings to find out which animals with backbones the meat-eating mammals had eaten (Shehzad et al., 2012). First, we mixed each sample with a liquid called a sodium phosphate lysis buffer for 15 minutes, which breaks open the cells and releases their DNA. We then pulled out all the DNA and dissolved it in 400 μl of liquid, using the NucleoSpin Soil Kit (Macherey-Nagel, Germany).

Next, we made many copies of one particular stretch of DNA, called the 12S mitochondrial rRNA gene. This stretch differs between kinds of animals, so it works like a name tag. To copy it we used a method called PCR (polymerase chain reaction), which copies a chosen piece of DNA over and over. We used a primer called 12SV5 (Riaz et al., 2011), a short piece of DNA that marks where copying should start. This primer works for almost all animals with backbones. We ran each sample three times, as three separate copies of the PCR, called replicates.

Fox, marten and badger DNA can also be copied by mistake, so we added blocking oligonucleotides, which are short pieces of DNA that stop the copying of the animal's own DNA. This only partly blocked the copying, so we could still tell which animal the droppings came from (see Text S2 in Appendix S1; Vestheim & Jarman, 2008). We did the DNA extraction and copying in separate rooms, each used only for this work. The company Fasteris (Geneva) then read the DNA sequences on a NextSeq 500 machine (Illumina, USA).

We analysed the DNA readings with a computer program called OBITools (Boyer et al., 2016). First, we removed sequences that had been read only once, that contained unclear letters, or that were too short or too long (shorter than 60 or longer than 130 bp, where bp, or base pairs, are the letters of DNA). We also removed groups of matching sequences, called molecular taxonomic units (MOTUs), that did not reach 10 reads in at least one PCR replicate.

We then named the remaining sequences by comparing them with two reference libraries of known DNA: one local and one worldwide, built from the European Nucleotide Archive of EMBL (http://www.ebi.ac.uk/embl/). We kept only matches that were at least 95% identical. At this stage we also found and removed contamination, which was mostly DNA from primates, and tag jumps, where a sequence had been given the wrong PCR label during reading.

To decide which animal each sample came from, we used a kind of voting system. An animal had to be the most common of all the possible animals in at least two of the three PCR replicates, and it also had to make up at least 1% of the reads in that replicate. We then checked the results by hand. We fixed sequences that had not matched well, names that were wrong or repeated (for example, Microtus and Microtus agrestis), and names that were not at the level of species. When several MOTUs were named as the same animal and appeared in the same PCR replicate, we added their reads together. In the rest of the analysis, we only used animals that made up at least 1% of the reads on average across the PCR replicates (Deagle et al., 2019). Appendix S1 (Text S2) gives more details on the lab work, the computer analysis and the checking by hand.

### 2.4 Analysing the results

To describe how often dogs and field voles appeared in the diet of foxes and martens, we used two measures. The first was the percentage frequency of occurrence (% FO): the share of droppings that contained the animal. The second was a modified relative read abundance (RRA): the average percentage of reads that belonged to that animal across the droppings in which it was found.

We wanted to test whether foxes used dog droppings as a backup food when voles were scarce. To do this, we used three statistical models called generalized linear models. These are tools that estimate how the chance of something happening changes with other factors. Here, the thing we were looking at was whether dog DNA was present or absent in a fox dropping, which is a yes-or-no outcome. We treated it as a binomial random variable, a standard way of handling yes-or-no outcomes. We also treated the four seasons, one after another, as separate categories.

In each model, we looked at how the chance of dog DNA in fox droppings changed with the percentage frequency of occurrence of field voles. We put the sampling season and the field vole measure into separate models, because they were so closely linked that it would have been hard to tell their effects apart. Within each season, we combined the data for each site, giving three to six sites per season.

We treated each site as a separate, independent repeat of the study. To check this, we tested for spatial autocorrelation, which is when samples close together are more alike than samples far apart, using the "testSpatialAutocorrelation" function in the "DHARMa" package for the R software (Florian, 2021; R Core Team, 2021). We ran two models for this. The first used a simple yes-or-no outcome (whether dog DNA was present or absent) and the sampling season as a category. The second used the same things but also allowed each site to have its own starting level, called a random intercept, so that some sites could simply have more dog DNA than others. We fitted it with the "glmer" function in the "lme4" package (Bates et al., 2022).

We used "DHARMa" to check that the models fitted the data well. It looked at whether the leftover differences between the model and the data (the residuals) were spread evenly, whether they were more spread out than expected (overdispersion), and whether there were any unusual values (outliers). For the field vole model, we saw some departures from the expected pattern, but these were not statistically significant overall, and the model's assumptions were met. We present each model's estimates together with their 95% confidence intervals, which are ranges that show how uncertain each estimate is.

We also wanted to check whether the dog DNA sequences were just mistakes made from fox DNA. We compared the sequences of the MOTUs named as fox (6) and as dog (21), using the "adist()" function in the "utils" package. We then plotted the number of dog and field vole DNA reads per PCR (1941 in total, from 647 fox droppings × 3 PCR replicates) against the number of fox reads per PCR. We fitted 90th quantile regressions over the part of the data where there were reads, using the "rq" function in the "quantreg" R package (Koenker, 2021). A quantile regression fits a line through a chosen part of the data, here the upper 10%, so it shows the highest values rather than the average. Before plotting and fitting, we took the logarithm (base 10) of the number of reads, plus the smallest read count found in the data. We did all the data handling, analysis and graphs in R 4.0.5.

### 2.5 Measuring the energy in dog droppings

To find out how much energy fresh dog droppings contain, we tested samples from six dogs and households whose dogs ate a range of dry and wet dog foods bought in shops. We measured the energy by burning the samples in a sealed container and measuring the heat, a method called calorimetric explosion (Hambly & Speakman, 2005).

We weighed each sample before and after drying it at 60°C for 14 days, which told us what percentage of it was water. We then blended the samples into an even mixture and pressed them into small pellets of 0.15–0.25 g. We calibrated the machine with benzoic acid, a chemical whose energy content is already known. We then burned each pellet in a Parr 6100 calorimeter, using an 1108 oxygen bomb (Parr Instrument Company, USA). We tested each sample 2–4 times, until the results varied by less than 1.5% of their average (the relative standard deviation).

We present the results as megajoules of energy per kilogram of dry and wet weight, and as kilocalories per 100 g of dry and wet weight. For four of the six dogs, we also weighed the mineral material left over after burning, which cannot burn. We give this as a percentage of the weight of the wet and dry pellets. To work out the wet weight of the pellets from their dry weight, we used the average water content of the dog droppings in this study, which was 60.5%.
parts.results:
## 3 Results

Our DNA test identified 647 samples as red fox, and these gave us information about what the foxes had eaten. In these fox samples, dog DNA turned up in 39.1% and field vole DNA in 55.2% (Table 1).

We also worked out how much of the fox diet each animal made up, using a measure called relative read abundance (RRA). It compares how many copies of an animal's DNA the test read with the total number of DNA copies read from all the animals in the sample. By this measure, dog made up 26.5% of the fox diet and field vole 65.4%.

We did the same for pine martens, using 1060 samples. Here we report a second measure, frequency of occurrence (FO), which is simply the percentage of samples in which an animal's DNA was found. Dog DNA appeared in 0.85% of pine marten samples and field vole DNA in 56.51%. By relative read abundance, dog made up 14.6% of the pine marten diet and field vole 71.21%.

TABLE 1

How often field vole and dog DNA turned up in red fox and pine marten droppings (frequency of occurrence, FO, %), and how much of each animal's diet each prey made up (modified relative read abundance, RRA, %).

| Predator | Prey | Number of times found | Number of samples (N) | FO (%) | RRA (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Red fox (Vulpes vulpes) | Field vole (Microtus agrestis) | 357 | 647 | 55.18 | 65.38 |
| | Dog (Canis lupus familiaris) | 253 | | 39.1 | 26.51 |
| Pine marten (Martes martes) | Field vole (Microtus agrestis) | 599 | 1060 | 56.51 | 71.21 |
| | Dog (Canis lupus familiaris) | 9 | | 0.85 | 14.6 |

### 3.1 Could the dog DNA be a mistake in the lab?

To check this, we compared the fox DNA and dog DNA sequences, letter by letter. On average they differed at 7.68 positions (give or take 1.73), and the difference ranged from 4 to 12.

To read the DNA, we first made many copies of it in the lab using a method called PCR. Each copy of a sample is called a PCR, and each short piece of DNA the test reads is called a read. The more fox reads a PCR produced, the more dog reads it could produce at most (Figure 1a). We measured this upper limit as the 90th quantile: the value that 90% of the PCRs fell below. This pattern happens because the most reads any one animal, including the fox itself, can reach in a PCR rises as the total number of reads in that PCR rises (Figure S1 in Appendix S1).

Even so, 66% of the PCRs had no dog reads at all, and these were spread across the whole range of fox read numbers (Figure 1a). Field voles, the fox's main prey, were missing from 52% of the PCRs, which is a similar pattern (Figure 1b).

FIGURE 1

Number of dog DNA reads (a) and field vole DNA reads (b) compared with the number of red fox DNA reads, for each PCR. There were 1941 PCRs in total (647 fox droppings, each tested three times). We added one read to every sample and then took the base 10 logarithm, a way of squeezing very large and very small numbers onto one scale. The gray dashed lines split the data into four areas: no reads of either species (bottom left); dog reads (a) or vole reads (b) but no fox reads (top left); no dog or vole reads but fox reads (bottom right); and reads of either species (top right). The solid black lines show the 90th quantile, the upper limit of dog or vole reads, for PCRs with at least one read.

### 3.2 Are foxes eating dog droppings as a backup food?

We estimated the chance that dog DNA was present in a fox dropping, and we call this the probability of occurrence. In winter 2018 it averaged 0.24, with a range of 0.18 to 0.31. This was statistically significantly lower than in the three seasons that followed (p < .01; Table S1 in Appendix S1). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone; here, less than 1% of the time. In spring 2018 the average was 0.39 (range 0.32 to 0.46), in winter 2019 it was 0.49 (0.42 to 0.55), and in spring 2019 it was 0.48 (0.37 to 0.58) (Figure 2a).

Field vole DNA showed the opposite pattern. In winter 2018 it was present in fox droppings with an average probability of 0.93 (0.88 to 0.96). This was statistically significantly higher (p < .01; Table S1 in Appendix S1) than in the three seasons that followed. In spring 2018 it fell to 0.68 (0.61 to 0.74), dropped to its lowest point in winter 2019 at 0.19 (0.14 to 0.25), and then rose slightly to 0.36 (0.27 to 0.47) by spring 2019 (Figure 2a).

The two also moved in opposite directions. The more often field vole DNA turned up in fox droppings, the less likely dog DNA was to be there, and this link was statistically significant (p < .01; Table S1 in Appendix S1). When voles were absent, the probability of dog DNA was 0.56 (0.48 to 0.63). When voles turned up in 97% of fox samples, it fell to 0.27 (0.22 to 0.33) (Figure 2b).

FIGURE 2

Results from a generalized linear model, a statistical method that predicts how one measurement changes with others. (a) Predicted probability that dog DNA (black circles) and field vole DNA (gray triangles) were present in red fox droppings, for each sampling season and across sites. The lines show the 95% confidence interval, the range in which the true value is likely to lie. The number of fox samples in each season is printed at the bottom. (b) Predicted probability of dog DNA in red fox samples as field vole frequency of occurrence changes. The shaded area shows the 95% confidence interval. In both panels, the gray circles show the raw data for dog frequency of occurrence, with each point weighted by how many samples it came from.

### 3.3 Do dog droppings hold a lot of energy?

On average, dog droppings held 135.02 kilocalories (kcal) of energy in every 100 g of wet droppings. That is 345.57 kcal in every 100 g of dry droppings, once the water is removed (Table 2).

We also looked at the mineral content, meaning material that cannot burn. In four of the six dogs we tested, it made up 12.1% of the wet weight of the droppings (range 7.6% to 19.5%). In the same four dogs, it made up 30.7% of the dry weight (range 17.7% to 51.8%).

TABLE 2

Energy content of dog droppings, estimated from samples of six dogs from six households (N).

| Species | N | Megajoules per dry kg | Kilocalories per dry 100 g | Megajoules per wet kg | Kilocalories per wet 100 g |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dog (Canis lupus familiaris) | 6 | 14.47 ± 2.20 | 345.57 ± 52.52 | 5.65 ± 1.65 | 135.02 ± 39.34 |

| Species | N | Mineral content: % of dry pellet weight | Mineral content: % of wet pellet weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dog (Canis lupus familiaris) | 4 | 30.7 | 12.1 |

Note: Energy is given in megajoules per kilogram of dry and wet droppings, and in kilocalories per 100 g of dry and wet droppings. Mineral content is the average percentage of the dry and wet weight of the droppings that did not burn. We worked out the wet weight from the dry weight using the average water content of the dog droppings in this study (60.5%). Mineral data are available only for four dogs.
parts.discussion:
## 4 Discussion

Our results fit with the idea that the droppings of pet dogs are a valuable backup food for wild red foxes, and this could matter in important ways. Dog was the second most common animal we found in fox droppings. It turned up in 39% of all the fox droppings we collected, and in 48.5% of those collected in the season when field voles were scarcest.

In the study area, encouraging activities such as dog walking is one of several goals for managing the land. The others include growing timber and protecting wildlife. Dog walking may therefore give red foxes a source of food from outside their usual prey that nobody had recognised before. In this setting, we propose that foxes eating dog droppings as a backup food is best described as a form of commensalism, where one species benefits and the other is not affected. If this behaviour also happens between other animals, it could be a form of commensalism that has been overlooked. And if it is widespread, it could make the web of links between species more complicated by connecting species that would otherwise have nothing to do with each other. It could also act as a steadying force that helps communities cope when their surroundings change. To understand how big these effects are, though, we first need to know how common this habit is across different communities of living things.

The dog DNA in fox droppings did not come from mistakes in our lab work. The DNA test reads short stretches of DNA, called sequences, and dog sequences differed from fox sequences by more than 4%. That is far more than the errors we would expect from our sequencing runs. Averaged across the four sequencing lanes (the four separate runs of the machine), 88% of the DNA reads had an error rate of 0.1% or less. Also, whether dog DNA appeared, and how many dog DNA reads there were, was unrelated to the fox. Both results point to real dog DNA as the source.

We cannot formally rule out other sources of dog DNA, such as dogs urinating on fox droppings or rolling over them. However, dog DNA became more common at the same time as field voles became less common, and the two moved in opposite directions, a statistically significant link. (A link is called statistically significant when a pattern this strong would rarely appear by chance alone if there were really no link.) This makes the idea that foxes were eating dog droppings better supported. These results also suggest that foxes turn to this outside food when their main prey is scarce.

It is not technically impossible that foxes were getting dog DNA by killing or eating dogs, but we did not consider this a good enough explanation. In Australia, where red foxes have spread from elsewhere, dogs have been recorded in their diet. There, the evidence points indirectly to pet dogs rather than to the dingo, a closely related wild dog (Brunner et al., 1991; Fleming et al., 2021). Even where dogs have been reported, it is usually put down to foxes eating dogs killed on roads, although eating droppings has not been ruled out. Also, the share of fox droppings containing dog DNA in those studies was smaller than in ours. For example, one study found it in 0.34% of fox droppings (Fleming et al., 2021).

We found dog DNA in 39.1% of fox droppings. To get that high a share, foxes would need either an unrealistically large supply of dog carcasses (for example, roadkill left lying around), frequent attacks on dogs, or both. Such events would not go unnoticed by the public and the media (see Murugesu, 2021). In addition, dog DNA made up only a small share of the DNA reads in samples that contained dog DNA, compared with the same share for field voles. This suggests the source held little DNA, which fits with eating droppings rather than eating flesh rich in DNA (Table 1). Some uncertainty about the true rate remains, but taken together, we confidently conclude that our analyses show red foxes eating the droppings of pet dogs.

The DNA test in droppings has revealed a food source for the red fox that was otherwise overlooked. The red fox is a very well-studied species that often lives close to people and their dogs (Handler et al., 2019; Soe et al., 2017). Dog droppings contain no hard remains, such as bones, that could be picked out by hand. Foxes also eat many kinds of food, and many of the species they share their home with. This makes it almost impossible to spot foxes eating other species' droppings by sorting through the remains of their prey (Macdonald, 1987a; Tercel et al., 2021).

Even so, three earlier studies that used the DNA test in droppings to study red fox diet did not report dog either (Nørgaard et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2021; Xinning et al., 2019). This might be because dog walking was less common in their study areas, or because they had fewer droppings: 72, 3 and 103, compared with 647 in ours. Or, as with human DNA in our study, dog DNA may have been assumed from the start to be contamination. Interestingly, human droppings are also found all over our study area, for example from wild campers, and could have added human DNA to the samples.

Where we can rule out foxes directly eating dogs, the DNA test in droppings offers a way to find foxes eating other species' droppings that would otherwise stay hidden. Anyone using computer filters to sort the DNA results should keep this possibility in mind. Still, future work should check these findings in the field, by pairing them with direct observation or with experiments, for example by comparing areas with and without dogs (van der Wal & Loonen, 1998).

Because foxes eating other species' droppings has gone unnoticed in such a well-studied species, it might be common in many places and among many kinds of animals. For example, besides the studies we mentioned in the introduction, nine species of animals with backbones were reported feeding at the latrines of giant otters (Pteronura brasiliensis Gmelin) in Brazil (Leuchtenberger et al., 2012). One could imagine a situation where most species use the droppings of other species living in the same area as a backup food.

In our study, we also found DNA from other animals. In fox droppings, we found pine marten (0.62% of fox droppings) and Eurasian badger (2.16%) DNA. In pine marten droppings, we found dog (0.85%) and fox (0.57%) DNA. In badger droppings, we found marten DNA (2.44%). Badger DNA in fox droppings followed a similar pattern over time to dog DNA, ranging between 1.14 and 4.65% of fox droppings. However, it turned up only rarely, and we could not rule out foxes killing or eating badgers, so we cannot draw further conclusions (Kidawa & Kowalczyk, 2011).

A wild member of the dog family regularly ate the droppings of a pet dog, but two members of the weasel family did not. This happened even though all of them had the same supply of dog droppings and the same ups and downs in voles. It may suggest that eating other species' droppings is more likely between closely related species. However, recorded cases include hoofed animals, birds, weasel-family animals and primates, so the studies do not support this idea (Gallant, 2004; Negro et al., 2002; Nishikawa & Mochida, 2010; van der Wal & Loonen, 1998). Instead, animals that eat other species' droppings seem to be ones that eat similar foods. Plant-eaters are more likely to eat the droppings of other plant-eaters (for example, Speakman et al., 2021), and fish-eaters eat the droppings of other fish-eaters (for example, Favero, 1996). Another possible explanation, which could work alongside these, is that wild animals eat other species' droppings, while animals that live near people use outside resources brought in by humans, including human droppings. A few species that live alongside people may take over these resources (Atickem et al., 2010; Vanak & Gompper, 2009).

Dog droppings held a lot of energy. Each 100 g of dog droppings, measured by the weight of the dog that produced them, contained 135.02 kcal. That is similar to a range of small rodents, which contain 137–170 kcal per 100 g of live weight (Fleharty et al., 1973). An average adult Scottish fox weighs 6.4 kg, and its energy needs go up and down between 400 and 800 kcal per day depending on the season (Kolb, 1978; Saunders et al., 1993). To meet these needs, a fox would need 10 to 30 small rodents a day (assuming each rodent weighs 20 g on average), or 300 to 600 g of dog droppings a day.

Foxes spend almost no effort searching for dog droppings compared with wild prey, so the energy they could gain from eating other species' droppings is large. Because dogs eat a rich diet, their droppings may also be high in amino acids (the building blocks of protein), vitamins and minerals (Table 2; Davies et al., 2017; Flachowsky, 1997). Droppings may also be easier to digest than some raw foods (Krief et al., 2004; Speakman et al., 2021). We cannot estimate how much dog droppings enter the system, but the number of visitors to the Cairngorms National Park rose from 1.3 million in 2004 to 2.1 million in 2019 (MacDonald, 2020). Together with the fact that dog DNA was common in fox droppings, this suggests that dog droppings may be a rich, (increasingly) plentiful and harmless food source.

Red foxes usually specialise in small rodents when these are plentiful, and switch to other prey when they are scarce (Breisjøberget et al., 2018; Kjellander & Nordström, 2003). In areas with plenty of food, switching prey may let foxes avoid the boom-and-bust cycles of their main prey (Breisjøberget et al., 2018; Erlinge, 1987). Foxes certainly do well in landscapes changed by people. There, they are reported to live in small home ranges, and using food and other resources provided by people is part of how they have adapted (Handler et al., 2019; Jahren et al., 2020; Macdonald, 1987b). More and more people visiting remote areas may, without meaning to, feed fox populations and help them avoid depending on their main prey, even in areas with little food. The possible harm this extra food does to the animals foxes compete with, and to their prey, should be considered alongside the direct disturbance that visitors cause to wildlife (Hughes & Macdonald, 2013; Shutt & Lees, 2021).

Eating droppings clearly carries a risk of catching diseases or parasites, because animal droppings, including dog droppings, can carry large numbers of germs (Otranto et al., 2015; Raue et al., 2017; Sager et al., 2006; Xhaxhiu et al., 2010). Over time, the chance of picking up at least one parasitic worm, a single-celled parasite (or other germs such as canine distemper) by eating other species' droppings is likely high. Some of these germs are common in fox populations in Europe and the United Kingdom (Gillespie et al., 1956; Otranto et al., 2015; Richards et al., 1995; Sager et al., 2006). With people and animals travelling around the world, eating other species' droppings may expose wild animals to new germs (Messenger et al., 2014).

However, these risks should be weighed against the risks of not eating droppings, which may include starving, and the risk of infection in other ways. For example, parasites such as the fox tapeworm (Echinococcus multilocularis) can spread in the same ways as other germs, but also by being eaten in the wrong stage of life, or in a carrier animal that does not develop the parasite, as well as directly from droppings to mouth. Other parasites are carried by insects and similar animals (Otranto et al., 2015; Raoul et al., 2015). Also, wild animals can often carry a moderate number of parasites without showing any signs of illness (Thompson et al., 2010).

So, compared with the real energy gained (see above), eating other species' droppings may be a fairly small extra cost. Indeed, studies of animals that eat other species' droppings and checked their health found no related illnesses, although there is still little evidence (Butler et al., 2018; Krief et al., 2004). On the other hand, the animal being eaten may disturb or injure the one eating it. When this has been recorded, it is rather mild and unlikely to affect the population (Nishikawa & Mochida, 2010; Seguel et al., 2017; van der Wal & Loonen, 1998).

We therefore suggest that, in this case, the possible gains of eating other species' droppings seem to outweigh the possible downsides. We propose that foxes eating dog droppings as a backup food is best described as a form of commensalism. However, the balance between benefits and risks will change depending on how many kinds of germs are around and how common they are. Where pet dogs are involved, it will also depend on how many dogs are vaccinated.
